The Bergama barb (Capoeta bergamae) is a freshwater cyprinid endemic to the northwestern Anatolian river systems, where it typically inhabits fast-flowing, well-oxygenated streams. Field surveys have documented that females attain a total length at puberty of 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm], a relatively modest size compared to other members of the genus Capoeta. This species exhibits a protracted juvenile phase, during which individuals accumulate somatic reserves before redirecting resources toward gonad development. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], averaged 12% [GSI = 12%]. Histological examinations of ovarian tissue from gravid females confirm that oocyte development proceeds synchronously, with vitellogenesis initiating in early spring as photoperiod increases.

Eggs of Capoeta bergamae are demersal and adhesive, deposited over gravel substrates in shallow riffles during the spawning period. Upon fertilisation, the fertilised ovum undergoes rapid cleavage, and the resulting yolk-laden egg measures approximately 0.9 mm in diameter. The wet weight at birth, estimated from this egg size assuming spherical geometry and a density of 1.0 g per cubic centimeter, is 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a value consistent with the small egg sizes documented in other rheophilic cyprinids. Incubation duration is temperature-dependent, with hatching occurring after roughly 5 to 7 days at the thermal regime typical of spring headwaters. The prolarvae that emerge are lecithotrophic, subsisting entirely on endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days post-hatching. The newly hatched alevin measure only a few millimeters in total length and remain hidden within interstitial spaces of the gravel bed until yolk absorption is complete and the mouth becomes functional, marking the onset of exogenous feeding.

Growth trajectories derived from scale annuli and length-frequency distributions indicate that ultimate total length in wild populations reaches 19.8 cm [Li = 19.8 cm], representing the maximum size attained by this species under natural conditions. The corresponding ultimate wet weight associated with this length is 82.2 grams [Wwi = 82.2 grams], obtained from a length-weight regression fitted to field-captured specimens. These asymptotic dimensions position Capoeta bergamae among the smaller-bodied members of its genus, a distinction that may reflect selective pressures imposed by habitat fragmentation and seasonal drought in its native drainage basins. Mark-recapture studies conducted over a five-year period in the Bakırçay River system suggest that individuals approach their asymptotic length by the end of their third growing season. Somatic growth decelerates markedly thereafter, with energy increasingly diverted toward gonadal development and reproductive activities during the subsequent spawning seasons.

The wet weight at puberty, estimated from the length-weight relationship at the total length of 8 cm, is calculated to be 5.7 grams [Wwp = 5.7 grams]. This represents the minimum body mass at which individuals are capable of initiating gonadal recrudescence and participating in spawning events. Age at first reproduction has been inferred from otolith microincrement analysis, with most individuals attaining sexual maturity during their second calendar year. The lifespan of Capoeta bergamae has been determined through long-term tagging studies and validated by analysis of annuli from sagittal otoliths. Under the thermal conditions prevailing in its natural habitat, which approximate a mean annual water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded longevity is 6 years [am = 6 years]. This relatively short lifespan, characteristic of small-bodied cyprinids in dynamic lotic environments, results in a compressed reproductive window during which females must produce multiple clutches to ensure population persistence.

Reproductive output in Bergama barb is characterized by a combination of moderate fecundity and repeated spawning events within a single breeding season. Females produce approximately 800 to 1500 eggs per spawning event, with the exact number scaling positively with female body size. Field observations of marked individuals indicate that most reproductively active females complete two to three spawning events per year, typically coinciding with spring and early autumn high-flow periods that facilitate egg oxygenation and larval dispersal. Interannual variation in spawning frequency has been linked to variation in stream discharge and food availability, with females skipping reproductive activity entirely during drought years. The iteroparous strategy of Capoeta bergamae, combining moderate batch fecundity with multiple annual spawning events, contrasts with the semelparous life cycle observed in some congeners inhabiting more unpredictable environments.
